Snowflake (SNOW) stock fell 7.2% on Thursday, November 5, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 4.4%. What does Snowflake do, and did the stock fall on its own or with its group?

Snowflake is a technology company that operates the AI Data Cloud, a data platform for businesses. Management has tied the company's recent pickup in growth to AI. Product revenue grew 37% from a year earlier in fiscal Q2 2027, marking the third straight quarter in which growth sped up, management said on the September 2, 2026 call.

Newer products, such as AI functions and the AI gateway, contributed approximately half of that speed-up, management said on the same call. Citing strength in both its core data platform and its AI business, management also raised its product revenue forecast for fiscal 2027 to $6.07 billion. For a holder, the AI tie makes Snowflake partly a bet on businesses using AI on its platform.

While Snowflake fell more than the S&P 500, its drop was smaller than the 8.0% fall in the SPDR technology sector fund (XLK) that session. Among the peers Trefis tracks for Snowflake, Palantir Technologies fell 9.7%, while Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon.com and Alphabet all fell less than Snowflake. The stock moved with technology stocks as a group, not on its own.

CoreWeave Sinks 11%, Nebius Tumbles 9% as Hyperscaler Spending Jitters Rattle AI Cloud Stocks; Cloudflare Plunges 12%, Snowflake Drops 9%
sum: Microsoft and Alphabet spooked investors with surprise spending signals, and now four major AI cloud stocks are selling off hard as traders question who actually pays the bill when the biggest buyers of computing power start pulling back.

AI cloud stocks are falling again as investors rethink how much the biggest tech spenders will keep paying for outside computing power. CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock recently traded at $54.34, down 11%. The decline compounds a rough year for the graphics processing unit (GPU) cloud provider, which is now down 24% year to date (YTD).

Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS | NBIS Price Prediction) stock is at $156.73, down 9%. Even so, Nebius remains up 87% YTD. Like CoreWeave, Nebius is a so-called neocloud: a company that fills data centers with high-end AI chips and rents that computing power to AI labs and large tech firms. Because a handful of big customers sign most of the contracts, both companies depend heavily on those customers’ spending plans.
Microsoft and Alphabet Spending Signals Rattle the Neoclouds

Selling in the group stepped up after Microsoft reported capital spending that came in below expectations on October 28, sending CoreWeave and other neocloud stocks lower. For businesses that sell capacity to hyperscalers (the giant cloud operators), a slower Microsoft expansion raises the question of how much outside computing power the largest buyers will need.

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) unit Google followed with a record loss of market value, shedding more than $500 billion on October 29 after its report. Quarterly free cash flow at Google came in at negative $9.1 billion, worse than the negative $3.5 billion Wall Street analysts expected.

Evercore ISI strategist Julian Emanuel expects the hyperscaler cohort to stay cash-negative, with losses near $200 billion over the next year. That outlook matters for CoreWeave and Nebius, since buyers burning cash may push harder on price or slow new contracts while both neoclouds borrow heavily to build ahead of demand.

SpaceX Stock Is Down 23% From Its Post-IPO High. History Says This Will Happen Next. (Hint: It's a Big Move.)
sum: Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +8.62%) made its market debut on June 12. It was the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history by two different measures. The company raised a record $75 billion, and the stock started trading with a record market capitalization of nearly $1.8 trillion.

SpaceX shares hit an all-time high of $202 on June 16, representing 50% upside from its IPO price of $135. That brought its market value to $2.6 trillion. But the stock has since tumbled 23% to $156 as of June 23.

Wall Street sees that as a buying opportunity. The median target price (from eight analysts) is $238.50 per share, implying 53% upside from the current price. But history says SpaceX stock will decline sharply in the coming months.
History says SpaceX stock could drop sharply in the coming months

IPO stocks frequently pop on the first trading day. Since 1980, more than 9,000 companies have listed shares on U.S. stock exchanges, and their share prices increased by an average of 19% on day one, according to Jay Ritter, finance professor at the University of Florida.

SpaceX fit that pattern perfectly. The stock closed 19% higher on the first trading day. But its recent backslide fits another historical pattern. Large IPOs have typically dropped sharply during their first year on the public market. The following chart illustrates that point. It includes the 15 largest U.S. IPO stocks (by market value at the IPO price) since 2006.

Among the 15 largest IPOs in the past two decades, the average stock fell 50% from its IPO price at some point during the first year. And the average stock was still 33% below its IPO price at the end of the first year.
